content_voiceover: This algorithm is essentially the boards' preferred workup for a microcytic anemia when you suspect thalassemia. You start with RBC indices, and the branch point is MCV 78 and MCH 27. Above those cutoffs is normal, essentially ruling out thalassemia trait. Below those cutoffs, you move to hemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC, and this is where the numbers really matter for exam purposes. An HbA2 of 3.5% or higher with HbF 1 to 5% points to beta-thalassemia trait, the single most commonly tested pattern. An HbA2 under 3.5% with a low HbF and normal iron studies points toward alpha-thalassemia, since alpha thalassemia trait characteristically has a normal or even low HbA2, unlike beta thalassemia trait. A markedly elevated HbF, 5 to 20%, with a low HbA2 suggests beta-thalassemia major, delta-beta thalassemia, or hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin, HPFH. And an abnormal hemoglobin variant on HPLC steers you toward HbCS or HbE. The critical pearl: always confirm alpha thalassemia and rule out iron deficiency before finalizing the diagnosis, since iron deficiency can also lower MCV and mimic thalassemia trait, but with a normal HbA2. Definitive diagnosis in ambiguous cases relies on DNA analysis or the alpha to beta globin synthesis ratio.
keypoints: Screen: MCV <78, MCH <27 → suspect thalassemia, run HPLC/electrophoresis
HbA2 <3.5% + normal iron → α-thalassemia (normal/low HbA2 is the clue)
HbF 5-20% + low HbA2 → β-thal major, δβ-thal, or HPFH
Confirm with DNA analysis or α/β synthesis ratio
keypoint_voiceover: For thalassemia diagnosis, remember the microcytic screen at MCV 78 and MCH 27 triggers hemoglobin HPLC. The signature pattern for beta-thalassemia trait is HbA2 3.5% or higher with mild HbF elevation. Alpha-thalassemia classically shows a normal or low HbA2, which is the key differentiator, and you must rule out iron deficiency first. Markedly elevated HbF with low HbA2 suggests beta-thal major or HPFH, and definitive confirmation always comes down to DNA analysis.
